properties.name: Oro Junta
properties.basis: The junction with the line from Canon City, opened in 1900. The timetable of December 1907 prints Oro Junta 7.3 miles from Canon City. On the 1 m lidar a dead-straight embankment, cut through at the creek, runs north-east across the flats to the main line at the mouth of Phantom Canyon just here, and benches fork from the main line: taken to be the Canon City line and its junction. The exact place along the line is from the driving distances in N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found, checked against the two tunnels; his milepost (6.8 from Florence) would put it 1,650 ft further up the canyon.
properties.summary: Junction of the Florence and Cripple Creek with its line from Canon City, at the mouth of Phantom Canyon; from an embankment on the lidar and a secondary guide.

properties.name: Cramer
properties.basis: A helper-engine base built in 1902 with a siding, wye and telegraph office, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed by his driving distance, checked against the two tunnels, which agrees with his milepost to 50 ft once his mileposts' unexplained 0.24 mile excess over the survey south of Adelaide is taken off. The bench along the line is two to three times its usual width for half a mile here, which may be the yard or only the open canyon mouth.
properties.summary: A siding and helper base of 1902 near the foot of Phantom Canyon, from a secondary guide.

properties.name: Russell (Alabaster until 1895)
properties.basis: A water tank and short siding for helper engines at the foot of the canyon, given up for Cramer in 1902, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed by his driving distance and his milepost, which agree to 10 ft but are both his. A short wide bench stands at the spot on the lidar.
properties.summary: A water tank and siding at the foot of Phantom Canyon to 1902, from a secondary guide.

properties.name: Adelaide (first site, to the flood of 1895)
properties.basis: The Florence and Cripple Creek's timetable of 2 June 1895 prints Adelaide, a telegraph station, 17.4 miles from Florence. The pin is at 17.4 miles by the stationing of the railway's own survey of 1894, which the timetable's miles match (the Victor depot is 34.56 miles by stationing and 34.6 in the timetable). That falls on the surveyed line on the valley floor, 325 ft from the present road, and 124 ft from the mouth of East Fork Eightmile Creek. N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found, says this first Adelaide was destroyed by the flood of 30 July 1895 and the station rebuilt down the canyon. The pin stood 1,100 ft from here before, measured along the atlas's line, which is shorter than the surveyed one. Newspapers of the time (read on the page images) bear out the flood: on the evening of 30 July 1895 a cloudburst carried away the hotel at Adelaide and drowned three people in it, Mrs. Carr the landlady, Lee Tracy and a man named Watson (Rocky Mountain News and Colorado Daily Chieftain, 1 August 1895). None found says the station was moved; that still rests on Holmes. The first line here was patched and used until the high line opened on 27 June 1896, so the move, if there was one, may belong to 1896 and not 1895.
properties.summary: The first Adelaide, a telegraph station in the timetable of June 1895. The flood of 30 July 1895 carried away the hotel here and drowned three (newspapers of the time); that the station was then moved is from a secondary account.

properties.name: Adelaide (second site, 1895 to 1912)
properties.basis: The USGS names list puts 'Adelaide' here (a name from a 1950s map, not a survey of the station), and the driving distance in N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found, comes to within 200 ft of it; the pin is between the two, on the line, about half a mile down the canyon from the first site. He describes a depot, section house, tank and a siding of 1,192 ft, with foundations beside the road. His mileposts for this place do not fit (half a mile out). The bench is no wider here than elsewhere on the lidar. Newspapers of the time (read on the page images) bear out the flood: on the evening of 30 July 1895 a cloudburst carried away the hotel at Adelaide and drowned three people in it, Mrs. Carr the landlady, Lee Tracy and a man named Watson (Rocky Mountain News and Colorado Daily Chieftain, 1 August 1895). None found says the station was moved; that still rests on Holmes. The first line here was patched and used until the high line opened on 27 June 1896, so the move, if there was one, may belong to 1896 and not 1895.
properties.summary: Adelaide as rebuilt after the flood of 1895, by a secondary account; placed from the name on the government map. Whether it moved in 1895 or with the high line in 1896 is not known.

properties.name: Dale
properties.basis: A siding of 852 ft, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 20.4 on the 1894 survey's stationing, brought onto the atlas's line; his driving distance agrees to 300 ft. The survey here is itself good only to about 250 ft. It rests on that one secondary source: nothing on the lidar or any map held picks the place out.
properties.summary: A siding in Phantom Canyon, from a secondary guide.

properties.name: Glenbrook (Collins until 1895)
properties.basis: A siding of 1,051 ft, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 22.4 on the 1894 survey's stationing; his driving distance, a separate measure, comes to within 44 ft of it. A side canyon comes in from the west 450 ft to the north, where the bench widens; at the pin itself it does not.
properties.summary: A siding in Phantom Canyon, from a secondary guide; two of its figures agree.

properties.name: Wilbur
properties.basis: The Florence and Cripple Creek's timetable of 2 June 1895 prints Wilbur, a telegraph station, 25.3 miles from Florence. The pin is at 25.3 miles by the stationing of the railway's own survey of 1894, which the timetable's miles match, on the bench the present road follows on the south side of the valley. N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found, describes a depot, siding, tank and coaling dock with foundations north-west of the road, and his driving distance puts it 650 ft down the valley, where the floor is wide; the station is taken to lie between the two. The pin stood about 280 ft from here before, measured along the atlas's line. Note: the atlas's line here runs on the creek floor up to 100 ft from the surveyed bench.
properties.summary: A telegraph station in the Florence and Cripple Creek's timetable of 1895, in Phantom Canyon; placed by the railway's survey stationing.

properties.name: Loop
properties.basis: A siding of 909 ft between the two horseshoe curves, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 27.6 on the 1894 survey's stationing; his driving distance agrees to 400 ft. It does lie between the line's two horseshoes. It rests on that one secondary source: nothing on the lidar or any map held picks the place out.
properties.summary: A siding between the two horseshoe curves in upper Phantom Canyon, from a secondary guide.

properties.name: Alta Vista
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the line climbs at 3.5 to 3.8 per cent to this point and is level for the next 1.6 miles; benches join and leave the line just beyond, and the bench is up to 120 ft wide. N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found, calls Alta Vista the top of the four per cent grade and the end of the helper district, with yard tracks, a wye, depot and tank, and his driving distance falls here. His milepost (31.4) would put it 3,200 ft further on, where the bench is narrow and nothing joins it: not settled, hence the wide margin.
properties.summary: The head of the long climb out of Phantom Canyon, where helper engines were cut off; placed at the top of the grade on the lidar.

properties.name: Hollywood (South Victor)
properties.basis: A siding of 925 ft below a townsite also called South Victor, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 34.1 on the 1894 survey's stationing, which falls in a stretch of nearly half a mile where the bench is about 120 ft wide on the lidar. The USGS names list has 'Hollywood' 412 ft off the line a little further on.
properties.summary: A siding on the approach to Victor from Phantom Canyon, from a secondary guide; the bench is wide here.

properties.name: Eclipse (Florence and Cripple Creek)
properties.basis: The Florence and Cripple Creek's stopping place and the junction of its spur to the Elkton mine, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 36.1 on the 1894 survey's stationing, measured from both the Victor and the Cripple Creek depots (the two differ by 158 ft; the mean is used). It falls within 250 ft of the head of the survey's hairpin. The ground here has been mined away or buried, so nothing can be tested on it. The Midland Terminal had its own stopping place of this name on its own line, pinned separately 544 ft away; that pin is not moved.
properties.summary: The Florence and Cripple Creek's own stop at Eclipse, apart from the Midland Terminal's; from a secondary guide's milepost.

properties.name: Elkton (Florence and Cripple Creek; Arequa until 1895)
properties.basis: The Florence and Cripple Creek's station and two sidings, first called Arequa, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 36.9 on the 1894 survey's stationing, measured from both the Victor and the Cripple Creek depots (the two differ by 173 ft; the mean is used). The ground here has been mined away or buried, so nothing can be tested on it. The Midland Terminal had its own stopping place of this name on its own line, pinned separately 1,287 ft away; that pin is not moved.
properties.summary: The Florence and Cripple Creek's own station at Elkton, apart from the Midland Terminal's; from a secondary guide's milepost.

properties.name: Anaconda (Florence and Cripple Creek)
properties.basis: A small depot and a loading place for the Mary McKinney mine, according to N. D. Holmes's guide to the line for the Rocky Mountain Railroad Club (2013), a modern compilation from two books not held here; no company station list has been found. Placed at his milepost 38.4 on the 1894 survey's stationing, measured from both the Victor and the Cripple Creek depots (the two differ by 148 ft; the mean is used). The USGS names list has 'Anaconda (historical)' 144 ft off the line about 200 ft further along. The ground here has been mined away or buried, so nothing can be tested on it. The Midland Terminal had its own stopping place of this name on its own line, pinned separately 1,066 ft away; that pin is not moved.
properties.summary: The Florence and Cripple Creek's own stop at Anaconda, apart from the Midland Terminal's; from a secondary guide's milepost.

properties.name: West Beaver Creek trestle (Short Line)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 38.746554, -105.097863 and begins again at 38.746272, -105.099400, 545 ft apart, with the ground up to 81 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-sl-10). Low mounds stand on the valley floor under the line, which may be footings; not examined. Engineering News of 1 May 1902 (read on the page) calls the trestle over West Beaver Creek, two and a half miles east of Cameron, the longest and highest on the line, 500 ft long and 84 ft high, of timber on concrete piers, and says its piers were washed out in May 1901. That the opening here is that trestle is inferred from the creek's name, the distance from Cameron and the size; no map or photograph has been matched to it. The present road leaves the railway's line and goes round the head of the valley. Looked at again: the trestle ran crest to crest between benches with no approach fills, 486 ft against the 500 printed (a later writer gives 491); two low mounds 112 ft apart on the valley floor may be what is left of the concrete piers, not settled. No photograph of it has been found. Colorado Springs newspapers of 20 and 22 May 1901 (machine text, not checked on the page) say the flood took out the middle bent and three of the concrete piers and stopped traffic for about two days.
properties.summary: The Short Line's longest and highest trestle, across West Beaver Creek east of Cameron: 500 ft long and 84 ft high in the engineering press of 1902; the opening on the ground is 545 ft and 81 ft. Gone; the road goes round the head of the valley.

properties.name: Bear Creek trestle (Short Line)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 38.821437, -104.890923 and begins again at 38.820643, -104.889939, 427 ft apart, with the ground up to 72 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-sl-02). The written lengths are shorter than the opening: 336 ft in the National Register form for the Gold Camp Road, citing a newspaper of 1900 (secondary), and 340 ft in newspapers of 1910 (headlines and machine text only). The same accounts, not read on the page, say it burned about 2 April 1910 and was rebuilt in wood, and was burned again on 14 May 1918. That this opening is that trestle is inferred from the creek's name. Looked at again: the bench ends are slumped, and where the ground is 25 ft below grade the span is 337 ft, which is the written length; so the trestle probably ended about 45 ft inside each crest. It was curved (a later account), it crossed over the Bear Creek Canyon road, and the USGS sheet of 1948 draws a bridge here. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 this and the Silver Cascade bridge were the only two left in 1938. A later account (Westside Pioneer, 2014; secondary) calls this the railway's bridge 3-A, 60 ft high and 340 ft long. With the board '8A' photographed at mile board CS 8, that suggests bridges were numbered by the mile from Colorado Springs with a letter; inferred from two numbers only.
properties.summary: The Short Line's curved timber trestle over Bear Creek and its road at the edge of Colorado Springs: 336 to 340 ft in the written accounts, which fits the ground once the slumped bench ends are allowed for. Burned and rebuilt more than once; one of the last two standing, a road bridge as late as 1947.

properties.name: Adelaide Bridge (Florence and Cripple Creek Bridge No. 10)
properties.basis: The bridge stands and carries Phantom Canyon Road; its ends are taken from the modern map (OpenStreetMap way 42789435, 224 ft long), each good to about 30 ft, and on the 1 m lidar the creek is 57 ft below the grade here. The Colorado bridge inventory form of 1984 (a later account, from a field inspection in 1983; read on the page) describes a steel deck girder bridge of three 69 ft spans on two laced steel towers, 210 ft overall, calls it the railway's Bridge No. 10, gives its completion as April 1894, and places it in the south-west quarter of section 14, township 17 south, range 69 west, which is here. Doubt: the atlas takes the road hereabouts to be the high line of 1896 and puts the first line of 1894 on the valley floor, with the split between them unsure just here; a bridge of April 1894 at this height bears on that and has not been worked out. The date is the form's, not a record of the time.
properties.summary: The one railway bridge still standing in Phantom Canyon: a steel deck girder on two steel towers over East Fork Eightmile Creek, three spans of 69 ft, 210 ft overall, now carrying the road. Dated April 1894 by a later inventory form.

properties.name: Removed trestle or bridge, Colorado Midland, above Buena Vista (394 ft)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 38.864924, -106.136511 and begins again at 38.863891, -106.136152, 394 ft apart, with the ground up to 79 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-cm-39). A side valley 80 ft deep crossed straight between two graded approaches; opening natural ground. A high trestle is likely. No map, photograph or written record has been matched to this opening, so what stood in it, and when, is not known; the place name given is only a rough guide.
properties.summary: An opening in the Colorado Midland's grade 394 ft long and up to 79 ft deep, where a trestle or bridge has been removed. Found on the lidar; no record has been matched to it, and it has no name here.

properties.name: Removed trestle or bridge, Colorado Midland, east of Buena Vista (269 ft)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 38.833896, -106.055977 and begins again at 38.833504, -106.055177, 269 ft apart, with the ground up to 45 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-cm-42). Two embankments end either side of a creek; the line crosses straight; opening natural ground. No map, photograph or written record has been matched to this opening, so what stood in it, and when, is not known; the place name given is only a rough guide.
properties.summary: An opening in the Colorado Midland's grade 269 ft long and up to 45 ft deep, where a trestle or bridge has been removed. Found on the lidar; no record has been matched to it, and it has no name here.

properties.name: Removed trestle or bridge, Colorado Midland, east of Buena Vista (453 ft)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 38.834544, -106.046999 and begins again at 38.834227, -106.045484, 453 ft apart, with the ground up to 50 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-cm-44). A fill runs out to a sharp end at A over a valley; the other side climbs to a graded bench at B; opening natural ground. A removed trestle. No map, photograph or written record has been matched to this opening, so what stood in it, and when, is not known; the place name given is only a rough guide.
properties.summary: An opening in the Colorado Midland's grade 453 ft long and up to 50 ft deep, where a trestle or bridge has been removed. Found on the lidar; no record has been matched to it, and it has no name here.

properties.name: Removed trestle or bridge, Colorado Midland, near Leadville (295 ft)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 39.232931, -106.304393 and begins again at 39.232346, -106.305115, 295 ft apart, with the ground up to 35 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-cm-16). Two embankments end sharply either side of a gulch; the opening is natural ground. A removed trestle or bridge. No map, photograph or written record has been matched to this opening, so what stood in it, and when, is not known; the place name given is only a rough guide.
properties.summary: An opening in the Colorado Midland's grade 295 ft long and up to 35 ft deep, where a trestle or bridge has been removed. Found on the lidar; no record has been matched to it, and it has no name here.

properties.name: Removed trestle or bridge, Colorado Midland, east side of Hagerman Pass (400 ft)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the grade stops at 39.257503, -106.469012 and begins again at 39.256642, -106.469777, 400 ft apart, with the ground up to 38 ft below the grade line between them and nothing standing in the opening; the ends are where the ground comes back to the grade line, each good to about 20 ft (research/structures/bridges.md, br-cm-81). On the east side of Hagerman Pass: an embankment runs out to a sharp end at A on a curve; the line crosses a hollow on the curve to a cut at B. A removed curved trestle. Whether this is the trestle remembered as the great curved one is not tested. No map, photograph or written record has been matched to this opening, so what stood in it, and when, is not known; the place name given is only a rough guide. Whether this is the curved trestle remembered below Hagerman Pass (1,084 ft in later accounts) is not established: this opening is far shorter.
properties.summary: An opening in the Colorado Midland's grade 400 ft long and up to 38 ft deep, where a trestle or bridge has been removed. Found on the lidar; no record has been matched to it, and it has no name here.

properties.name: Colorado Midland short tunnel north of Tunnel 4 (Tunnel 5 on a supplied map)
properties.basis: Portals read from the 1 m lidar (26 November 2026): 38.871538, -104.928452 and 38.871763, -104.928752, 119 ft apart along the bore, good to about 10 and 10 ft. Both faces sharp; open cut of about 60 ft between its south face and the long bore's north face, 25 ft of it at grade. A portal is taken where the ground has risen a portal's height above the grade, so the length reads 5 to 15 per cent short of a measured tunnel where the faces are sharp (research/structures/tunnels.md). The line was redrawn through these portals on 26 November 2026. The number 5 is from a supplied Google Earth file whose maker is not known; a journal of 1887 gives 'Tunnel No. 5' as 515 ft, which this is not, so the number is doubtful. What is measured is the bore.
properties.summary: A short bore, 119 ft between the portals, a few yards north of the long tunnel the supplied map numbers 4. It had no pin of its own before.

properties.name: Hagerman Tunnel (Colorado Midland)
properties.basis: Portals read from the 1 m lidar (26 November 2026): 39.252363, -106.484100 and 39.255456, -106.489918, 1,995 ft apart along the bore, good to about 40 and 35 ft. Both ends rise gradually (16-19 m): portals buried or collapsed; no open cut at grade at either end on the lidar. A portal is taken where the ground has risen a portal's height above the grade, so the length reads 5 to 15 per cent short of a measured tunnel where the faces are sharp (research/structures/tunnels.md). The line as drawn passes up to 79 ft from the bore here and has still to be redrawn through the portals. The bore's line is OpenStreetMap's; the name is the map's. Its length is given as 2,164 ft in a later account (Railway and Locomotive Historical Society, 1935; other later figures run from 2,061 to 2,200). The years it was used are not entered: no record of the time has been read.
properties.summary: The Colorado Midland's first tunnel under the Continental Divide. 1,995 ft between the portals on the lidar, both ends buried or fallen in; 2,164 ft in a later account.

properties.name: Busk-Ivanhoe Tunnel (Colorado Midland; later the Carlton Tunnel)
properties.basis: Portals read from the 1 m lidar (26 November 2026): 39.263734, -106.498237 and 39.248805, -106.471417, 9,339 ft apart along the bore, good to about 35 and 35 ft. East (busk) end rises over about 10 m, west (ivanhoe) face fairly sharp; both ends meet approach cuts. A portal is taken where the ground has risen a portal's height above the grade, so the length reads 5 to 15 per cent short of a measured tunnel where the faces are sharp (research/structures/tunnels.md). The bore's line is OpenStreetMap's; the name is the map's. Its length is given as 9,398 ft in a later account (Railway and Locomotive Historical Society, 1935). The years it was used are not entered: no record of the time has been read.
properties.summary: The long tunnel that replaced the line over Hagerman Pass. 9,339 ft between the portals on the lidar; 9,398 ft in a later account.

properties.name: Eleven Mile Canyon tunnel, western of two (Colorado Midland)
properties.basis: Portals read from the 1 m lidar (26 November 2026): 38.915857, -105.449819 and 38.915859, -105.449421, 113 ft apart along the bore, good to about 15 and 15 ft. Both faces sharp; the road (forest road 96) runs through: consistent with an open road tunnel. A portal is taken where the ground has risen a portal's height above the grade, so the length reads 5 to 15 per cent short of a measured tunnel where the faces are sharp (research/structures/tunnels.md). The canyon road runs through it. No record of the time has been matched to it, and it has no number here.
properties.summary: A tunnel on the Colorado Midland's grade in Eleven Mile Canyon, now a road tunnel: 113 ft between the portals.

properties.name: Eleven Mile Canyon tunnel, eastern of two (Colorado Midland)
properties.basis: Portals read from the 1 m lidar (26 November 2026): 38.915866, -105.448475 and 38.915936, -105.447836, 184 ft apart along the bore, good to about 20 and 20 ft. Both faces sharp; the road passes through (bench continuous). A portal is taken where the ground has risen a portal's height above the grade, so the length reads 5 to 15 per cent short of a measured tunnel where the faces are sharp (research/structures/tunnels.md). The canyon road runs through it. Its portal heights read an implausibly steep grade, so one approach floor is misread; the positions are not affected. No record of the time has been matched to it. A third tunnel is remembered in this canyon and has not been found.
properties.summary: A second tunnel 400 ft east of the first in Eleven Mile Canyon, now a road tunnel: 184 ft between the portals. It was on no map held when found.

properties.name: Iron Springs bridge over Ruxton Creek (Colorado Midland)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the Colorado Midland's grade, coming down from Tunnel 3, turns onto a level terrace beside Ruxton Creek, and the bore of Tunnel 2 stands on the far bank; between the terrace's edge at 38.857442, -104.927886 and the bank below Tunnel 2 at 38.857040, -104.926748 there is no ground at grade for 371 ft, on a curve of about 280 ft radius, and today's ground is up to 53 ft below the grade line (the valley floor is built up, so the drop was probably greater). Each end is good to about 30 ft. Nothing of the bridge is seen on the lidar. Library catalogue records (captions only) have a steel 'Iron Springs Bridge' under construction about 1886 and a freight wreck on the 'Ruxton Avenue bridge' on 10 September 1909 with the ground '75 feet below'; Ruxton Avenue runs under this crossing, and the ground shows only one crossing hereabouts, so the two names are taken to be one bridge. That is inference. A later account says the bridge was cut up in 1964 (secondary, not checked). The lidar scan first put this crossing between Tunnels 2 and 1 (candidate br-cm-07), 790 ft east of here; the ground between those two bores is at grade and that was wrong.
properties.summary: The Colorado Midland's high steel bridge over Ruxton Creek at Manitou Iron Springs, on a curve between the terrace west of the creek and Tunnel 2: 371 ft between the ends, about 53 ft above today's ground. Gone.

properties.name: Silver Cascade trestle, at Tunnel 3 (Short Line)
properties.basis: The road crosses this hollow on a fill. On the 1 m lidar the natural ground beside the road lies up to 22 ft below the railway's grade line; it is below grade for 253 ft, between 38.786046, -104.906743 and 38.785752, -104.906028, and 15 ft or more below it for about 200 ft, which is the likelier length of a trestle. The lidar cannot tell a trestle later buried in fill from a fill the railway built. About ten photographs show one trestle running straight out of a portal of Tunnel 3 onto bare rock directly above Silver Cascade Falls, of about seven bents and about 40 ft at the deep end. On the lidar it is the south-east portal that opens onto a bare rock bowl falling 50 to 65 ft within 130 ft; the north-west portal opens onto a plain bench. So the trestle began at the south-east portal face (measured, 15 ft) and ran to where the pad ends (inferred, 60 ft). A library caption says 'west portal', which the ground does not bear out, and another says 'over North Cheyenne Creek': it crosses a side gulch. The fill pad hides the floor, so the lidar's 22 ft is less than the photographs' height. Firmly identified. The ends are good to about 60 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-10). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest.
properties.summary: The trestle the photographers liked best: straight out of the south-east portal of Tunnel 3 onto bare granite above Silver Cascade Falls. About 200 ft; the road now crosses on a fill pad. One of the last two standing, by-passed about 1941.

properties.name: Trestle 8A, at mile board CS 8 (Short Line)
properties.basis: The road crosses this hollow on a fill. On the 1 m lidar the natural ground beside the road lies up to 68 ft below the railway's grade line; it is below grade for 420 ft, between 38.791490, -104.897387 and 38.790606, -104.898251, and 15 ft or more below it for about 322 ft, which is the likelier length of a trestle. The lidar cannot tell a trestle later buried in fill from a fill the railway built. A photograph of the time (Harlan; Pikes Peak Library District 402-109) shows a curved trestle with guard rails over a deep gulch, the bridge board '8A' and the mile board 'CS 8' legible, and the High Drive road meeting the track at its upper end. This is the first deep gulch up the line from Tunnel 2, 8.05 miles from the Denver and Rio Grande depot by the atlas's line, and the High Drive joins the road just above it on the USGS sheet of 1948. Well identified; that bridges were numbered by the mile is a guess from this one board. The ends are good to about 50 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-08). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest.
properties.summary: A curved trestle over a deep gulch, the first above Tunnel 2: the railway's own boards '8A' and 'CS 8' can be read in a photograph of the time. About 320 ft and 68 ft high on the ground; now a road fill.

properties.name: High trestle at Tunnel 1 (Short Line)
properties.basis: The road crosses this hollow on a fill. On the 1 m lidar the natural ground beside the road lies up to 50 ft below the railway's grade line; it is below grade for 453 ft, between 38.798800, -104.883196 and 38.798822, -104.884658, and 15 ft or more below it for about 262 ft, which is the likelier length of a trestle. The lidar cannot tell a trestle later buried in fill from a fill the railway built. The Rocky Mountain News of 28 March 1901 prints an engraving captioned 'Tunnel No. 1 and High Trestle': a high curved trestle running into a portal of Tunnel 1. This hollow is beside that tunnel and the fill in it now stands about 50 ft high, where Engineering News says the largest fill on the line in 1902 was 50 ft high and 300 ft long. Identified from the engraving and the height of the fill: good, not certain. The ends are good to about 50 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-05). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest.
properties.summary: A high curved trestle running into Tunnel 1, drawn in a newspaper engraving of March 1901. About 260 ft and 50 ft high on the ground; now a road fill.

properties.name: Cathedral Park trestle, Bison Creek (Short Line)
properties.basis: The road crosses this hollow on a fill. On the 1 m lidar the natural ground beside the road lies up to 57 ft below the railway's grade line; it is below grade for 755 ft, between 38.735487, -105.031260 and 38.734793, -105.033437, and 15 ft or more below it for about 413 ft, which is the likelier length of a trestle. The lidar cannot tell a trestle later buried in fill from a fill the railway built. Photographs (McClure and others) show a curved trestle of nine or ten bents at Cathedral Park, and a later account puts a trestle over Bison Creek just past Tunnel 9, since filled. The hollow here, just beyond Tunnel 9, is below grade for 755 ft, far more than nine or ten 20 ft spans: the trestle (about 180 to 200 ft by the photographs) stood somewhere within it, with fills either side, and its own ends are not fixed. The ends given are those of the whole hollow. The place is firmly identified; the trestle's ends within it are not. The ends are good to about 50 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-37). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest. Caution (26 November 2026): the height given here was read from a fitted grade line since found to stand 10 ft or more above the road hereabouts, so it is probably too great by about that much. Not re-measured.
properties.summary: The curved trestle just past Tunnel 9 at Cathedral Park. Photographs show nine or ten bents, so about 180 to 200 ft; the hollow is below grade for much longer, so the fill now there is partly the railway's own approaches. Now a road fill.

properties.name: Double Horseshoe trestle, Little Fountain Creek (Short Line; one of two)
properties.basis: The road crosses this hollow on a fill. On the 1 m lidar the natural ground beside the road lies up to 62 ft below the railway's grade line; it is below grade for 755 ft, between 38.731871, -104.934418 and 38.730488, -104.936368, and 15 ft or more below it for about 558 ft, which is the likelier length of a trestle. The lidar cannot tell a trestle later buried in fill from a fill the railway built. The National Register form for the road (a later account) says two trestles at the Double Horseshoe on Little Fountain Creek are buried in the present fills. This is the largest fill there, up to 62 ft high over the creek, higher than any fill the railway had in 1902 by Engineering News. Which of the two trestles it is, and where the other was, is not known; no photograph has been matched. Probable, from the fill's height and the later account. The ends are good to about 50 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-19). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest.
properties.summary: One of the two trestles of the Double Horseshoe on Little Fountain Creek, said in a later account to lie buried in the fills. A fill up to 62 ft high; no photograph of it has been found.

properties.name: Rock Creek trestle, on the loop below Tunnel 7 (Short Line)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the railway's grade stops at 38.735456, -104.911086 and begins again at 38.735466, -104.911684, 171 ft apart, with the ground up to 42 ft below the grade line between them; the ground is 15 ft or more below grade for about 125 ft, the likelier length of the trestle itself. Nothing stands in the opening. The railway's line here is itself inferred (the loop redrawn on 26 November 2026), so the ends rest on that line. Photographs catalogued as the Rock Creek trestle show seven to nine bents in two storeys under a crag, which is 140 to 180 ft and 35 to 45 ft high: the opening here fits. A photograph also shows a small railway bridge over the stage road beside Tunnel 7's west portal; whether that is this structure or another is not settled. Moderately well identified; good only to about 60 ft because the line is inferred. The ends are good to about 60 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-16). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest. The Cripple Creek stage road (today's Old Stage Road) passes through this gap: on the 1 m lidar the road is at 8,962 ft and the railway's banks end at 8,997 and 9,007 ft, so the road went about 44 ft under the track. It is the only place near Tunnel No. 7 where the road passes under the railway, so the photograph catalogued as a railway bridge over the stage road by the tunnel's west portal is very likely this trestle (inferred).
properties.summary: Where the loop north-west of Tunnel No. 7 crossed Rock Creek: an opening of 171 ft, up to 42 ft deep. Photographs show a trestle of seven to nine bents under the crag called The Castles, which fits. The loop itself is inferred.

properties.name: Trestle at the North Cheyenne hairpin (Short Line)
properties.basis: The road's hairpin here has a radius of about 90 ft, which a train could not take, and on the 1 m lidar a flat-topped stub of bench at grade, about 65 ft long, points south across the hollow from the road's upper arm. So the railway crossed the hollow; that is inferred from the ground. Where exactly is conjecture. One curve of 236 ft radius drawn tangent to the bench either side runs along the stub and climbs at 3.0 per cent; on it the trestle is about 239 ft at grade, between 38.786572, -104.913499 and 38.785967, -104.913284, and up to 51 ft above today's ground. But that curve is about 24 degrees, and Engineering News of 1902 gives 16 degrees as the sharpest on the line. A 16 degree curve misses the stub by 75 ft, needs 3.8 per cent and a trestle of 419 ft, and lies up to 90 ft to the east. Neither fits everything, so the ends are good only to about 80 ft. An earlier reading here gave 224 ft and 64 ft from a straight line between the bench ends; the 64 ft was measured to the lowest ground under that line. Engineering News calls the trestles of North Cheyenne Canyon noteworthy. It is a different structure from the Silver Cascade trestle. No photograph has been matched to it (research/structures/shortline-trestles-2.md; shortline-hairpin-retrace.png). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest.
properties.summary: Where the road now doubles back round the head of a hollow by North Cheyenne Creek on a curve no train could take; a stub of the railway's bench points across it. The crossing is real; the trestle's line is conjecture: about 240 ft long and 50 ft high on the curve that fits the stub.

properties.name: Trestle site near Tunnel 6 (Short Line)
properties.basis: On the 1 m lidar the railway's grade stops at 38.742693, -104.905902 and begins again at 38.741878, -104.905159, 387 ft apart, with the ground up to 78 ft below the grade line between them; the ground is 15 ft or more below grade for about 259 ft, the likelier length of the trestle itself. Nothing stands in the opening. The drawn line crosses a deep gulch obliquely between a plain bench at one end and a short fill face at the other, while the road goes round the head. No photograph or written record has been matched to this site. Probable on the ground alone; unnamed. The ends are good to about 20 ft (research/structures/shortline-trestles.md, site sl-t-13). Engineering News of 1 May 1902 counts 31 timber trestles on the line, 6,456 ft in all, every one of 20 ft spans; it does not list them. By an eyewitness's letter of 1941 only two were left by 1938, the road builders having filled or by-passed the rest.
properties.summary: An opening in the grade near Tunnel 6 where the road goes round the head of a gulch: 387 ft at grade, up to 78 ft deep. No photograph or record has been matched to it.

properties.name: Wade's ranch on the stage road ('Wade City')
properties.basis: The government sheet of 1909 (1:125,000, surveyed 1906-07) prints 'Wade' with a building beside the road here; the pin is on the building drawn at the road, where today's road lies on the sheet's road to about 200 ft; good to about 500 ft. The sheet of 1893 names nothing here. Newspapers (machine text, not checked on the page) have a coach accident 'two miles from Wade's ranch' in April 1893, the place 'about eight miles above the city on the Cheyenne Mountain road' in 1900, and in 1914 'Dad' Wade, aged 85, as 'founder of Wade City on the stage road'; the earlier papers say ranch or place, and 'Wade City' looks like a nickname. No photograph of it has been found. The years are those of the newspaper mentions, not of the ranch's beginning or end.
properties.summary: Joel H. Wade's ranch and roadhouse, a stopping place for the Cripple Creek coaches about eight miles up the Cheyenne Mountain road. Placed from the building a small-scale map of 1909 draws at the road; good to about 500 ft.

properties.name: Cather Springs
properties.basis: Named on the government sheet of 1909 (1:125,000, surveyed 1906-07) and read off it, good to about 1,000 ft. Whether there was a house or resort is not established; nothing written about it has been read.
properties.summary: A spring named on the government map of 1909, beside the road that leaves the stage road at Rock Creek and runs south (today's Emerald Valley Road). Nothing more is known of it here.

properties.name: Seven Lakes (hotel, and a branch road of 1881)
properties.basis: The lakes are read off the government sheet of 1894 (1:125,000, surveyed 1892-93), good to about 1,000 ft; the hotel's own site is not fixed. A newspaper of August 1881 (machine text, not checked on the page) has the toll road extended from Beaver Park to Seven Lakes; the hotel of 1878 is from a later account of 1954. Off the stage road by some miles, and not on any railway.
properties.summary: The lakes below Pikes Peak that the Cheyenne Mountain road was built to reach before there was a Cripple Creek: a hotel is said to have been built in 1878 and a branch road came up from East Beaver Park in 1881.

properties.name: Where the Old Stage Road meets Gold Camp Road (the Short Line's grade)
properties.basis: The end of OpenStreetMap's Old Stage Road on Gold Camp Road; on the 1 m lidar both stand at about 9,034 ft, so the road met the railway on the level. That it crossed the track at grade here in the railway's time is inferred. The government sheet of 1909 draws its road through the railway's loop at this place.
properties.summary: The top of today's Old Stage Road, on the Short Line's loop over Rock Creek just west of Tunnel No. 7 and about a mile and a half south of St. Peter's Dome. Road and railway grade are level here.

properties.name: Stage road buried under the Short Line's fill at Summit
properties.basis: The west end of a road bench read from the 1 m and 0.5 m lidar (see the bench itself). The Short Line's fill lies across it with no opening seen, so the bench is older than the fill of 1900-01; that it is the Cripple Creek stage road rests on the government sheet of 1909, which draws the road hereabouts. Two faint lines west of the fill were not followed. Followed up: one of the two faint lines west of the fill starts exactly opposite this point on the same grade and becomes a plain abandoned road in the valley beyond the loop, so the road did run under where the fill now stands.
properties.summary: Where an abandoned road bench coming up the valley from the east runs into the foot of the railway's embankment at the Summit loop and stops, 55 to 60 ft below the track.

properties.name: Half Way house on the stage road (about here; not located)
properties.summary: The roadhouse where the Cripple Creek coaches stopped for meals, known from 1894 to 1906. It stood somewhere in East Beaver Park, at or within about a mile of Rosemont; its site has not been found and may be under the reservoir.
properties.basis: Not located; the pin marks the neighbourhood only. Four readings fall in East Beaver Park within about a mile and a third of each other along the road: a mining claim of 1894 'six miles below the half-way house' on East Beaver Creek; the Short Line's grading contracts of 1900, which were divided at the Half Way house 17 miles from Cameron, as Rosemont is by the railway's later timetable; a description of the railway's route passing it before the Beaver Creek valley; and half the road's length. A later account of 1954 calls Rosemont the half-way point. All but the last are newspapers read as machine text, not checked on the page. Against: the same contracts' 23 miles from Bear Creek canon falls three miles further west, and Mrs A. B. Love told F. W. Cragin in 1922 that it stood where John Love's ranch had been, on West Beaver Creek. It was offered for rent furnished in 1894; by 1900 it had meals, beds and a telephone; a coach overturned 'three and one-half miles east' of it 'in a steep grade' in 1896, which fits the climb out of Rock Creek. No picture of it has been found.

properties.name: Manitou depot (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: OpenStreetMap station node 7742140486 'Manitou Depot' (the 2021 depot on the old site); the 1948 sheet's BM 6570 stands beside it. Track at the platform 6,565 ft on the lidar. The railway's time card of 1915 (read on the page) gives Manitou as 8.90 miles from the summit, 6,562 ft. The railway's elevations of that day read about 100 to 140 ft above the lidar's all along the line. The first trains of 1891 are said to leave from 'Iron Springs' (newspapers, machine text). Insurance maps show a two-storey frame depot in 1892 and a stone ground floor in 1900.
properties.summary: The lower terminus of the cog road, on Ruxton Creek above the Iron Springs: 8.90 miles and 7,547 ft below the summit by the railway's time card of 1915.

properties.name: Minnehaha (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: Point on the line nearest the building lettered Minnehaha on the 1948 Manitou Springs sheet (the building stands 300 ft off the line, by BM 8332). Track 8285 ft. The time card of 1915 (read on the page) gives Minnehaha as 7.06 miles from the summit, 8,400 ft. The railway's elevations of that day read about 100 to 140 ft above the lidar's all along the line.
properties.summary: A stop on the cog road in Engelmann Canyon, 7.06 miles from the summit by the time card of 1915.

properties.name: Half-Way House (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: Three things put the Half-Way House here, within about 350 ft of one another along the line. A photograph in Richardson's paper of 1894 is captioned 'Hell-Gate, from Half-Way House. Station 324. Siding on the left' (read on the page); stations are feet from the summit on the level, and station 324 falls here when the 1894 profile is laid on the drawn line, a fit tested against the lidar to about 30 ft. The profile's 12.23 per cent grade, the steepest on which Richardson says switches were laid (machine text), runs from station 321+25 to 326+00, around this point. The time card of 1915 (read on the page) gives the Half-Way House as 6.27 miles from the summit, which is 2.63 miles of rail from Manitou and comes out 150 to 350 ft below this point; and its elevation, 8,913 ft, is on the profile at about station 327. The pin is at station 324. Until 27 Nov 2026 the pin stood 1,000 ft further up, where the map of 1948 letters 'Midway' and 'Water'; the track there is 120 ft higher than the time card's figure allows once the railway's datum is taken off, so 'Midway' is a later or a different stop. The profile letters 'Halfway Ho.' between the two, over stations 316+50 to 321+25: lettering, not a mark. Scientific American of January 1891 (machine text) has trains running this far in the autumn of 1890. No building was looked for on the ground.
properties.summary: The stop the first trains ran to in the autumn of 1890, 6.27 miles from the summit, with a siding. Placed at Station 324 of the 1894 survey. Not the Half Way house of the Cripple Creek stage road.

properties.name: Ruxton Park, first called Mountain View (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: 1948 sheet letters 'Old Mountain View' beside the line here; point on the line under it. OpenStreetMap siding 646441683 lies 500-900 ft further down. Track 9729 ft. The railway's tables of 1904 and 1908 (machine text) put Mountain View at 4.86 miles from the summit, 9,705 ft; the time card of 1915 (read on the page) calls that same point Ruxton Park and puts Mountain View higher. When the name moved was not found. The railway's elevations of that day read about 100 to 140 ft above the lidar's all along the line.
properties.summary: A stop 4.86 miles from the summit that the railway called Mountain View in 1904 and 1908 and Ruxton Park by 1915; 'Old Mountain View' on the map of 1948.

properties.name: Mountain View (Pikes Peak cog road; today's passing siding)
properties.basis: Middle of OpenStreetMap passing siding 646441684 (578 ft, 9,938-10,018 ft); the 1951 Pikes Peak sheet's BM 10013 at the sheet edge beside it. Track 9976 ft. The time card of 1915 (read on the page) gives Mountain View as 4.28 miles from the summit, 10,120 ft; newspapers of 1946 and 1947 (machine text) call it a water stop and the half-way lunch stop. The railway's elevations of that day read about 100 to 140 ft above the lidar's all along the line.
properties.summary: The stop and passing siding 4.28 miles from the summit by the time card of 1915; a water stop and lunch stop in the 1940s.

properties.name: Windy Point (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: 1951 Pikes Peak sheet letters Windy Point below the water tanks and spot height 12131 on the line; point on the line nearest the spot height. Track 12133 ft on the lidar. The time card of 1915 (read on the page) gives Windy Point as 2.25 miles from the summit, 12,232 ft. The railway's elevations of that day read about 100 to 140 ft above the lidar's all along the line. The officials' special of 30 June 1891 was stopped by a rockfall a short way above here (newspapers, machine text).
properties.summary: A stop above timberline, 2.25 miles from the summit by the time card of 1915, with water tanks close by.

properties.name: Summit of Pikes Peak (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: Centre of OpenStreetMap platform 1013894005 at the end of track (summit house of 2021); the 1951 sheet's Summit House 55 ft from the line's end. End of track 14,079 ft on the lidar. The time card of 1915 (read on the page) gives the summit as 14,109 ft; the railway's table of 1904 has 14,147. The railway's elevations of that day read about 100 to 140 ft above the lidar's all along the line. In 1891 the old signal station served as the dining hall (machine text). The time cards also list Saddle House (1.77 miles from the summit) and Butterworth Flat (7.74), which are not placed; Timber Line (2.87) has its own pin.
properties.summary: The upper terminus of the cog road. The first train reached it on 30 June 1891, by newspapers read as machine text.

properties.name: Ruxton Creek bridge at Minnehaha (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: OpenStreetMap tags this piece as a bridge (way 488256105, 27 ft) where the line crosses Ruxton Creek; the lidar shows the creek channel 10 ft below the grade under it, 39 ft between the banks. The ends, where the ground comes back to the grade line on the 1 m lidar, are at 38.849237, -104.955833 and 38.849201, -104.955963, good to about 10 ft each. The surest of the four: the modern map marks a bridge here. Richardson's paper of 1894, p. 419 (read on the page), has 'four iron bridges, two of 20 feet and two of 30 feet span' on granite masonry, and culverts 'all built of red spruce logs'; the Railroad Gazette of 4 April 1890 (read on the page) says the short bridges 'are all plate girders on masonry abutments' and that some stand on steep grades. No source found says where any of the four stands: Richardson's plan and profile, examined whole, draw no bridge, culvert or stream. One book of 1890, written before the line was finished, counts three bridges, not four (machine text, not checked on the page). This crossing falls at about station 376+46 of the 1894 profile (feet from the summit), on its 15.33 per cent grade. Ruxton Creek is the one stream the line crosses in the open, and it does so three times; these three open crossings are inferred to be three of the four iron bridges. Which are the 20 ft spans and which the 30 ft is not known. The line was rebuilt in 2018 to 2021, so what spans each opening today may not be what was built in 1890.
properties.summary: The cog road's bridge over Ruxton Creek below Minnehaha: 39 ft between the banks, about 10 ft above the creek.

properties.basis: A 7 ft deep, 33 ft gap in the ground under the track where a side gully from the south-east crosses; no stream is mapped through it and OSM tags no bridge. The bare-earth lidar shows an open channel, so the track spans it on a short bridge or an open-ended culvert: cannot tell which. The ends, where the ground comes back to the grade line on the 1 m lidar, are at 38.855325, -104.932347 and 38.855246, -104.932403, good to about 10 ft each. Bridge or open culvert: not told apart. Richardson's paper of 1894, p. 419 (read on the page), has 'four iron bridges, two of 20 feet and two of 30 feet span' on granite masonry, and culverts 'all built of red spruce logs'; the Railroad Gazette of 4 April 1890 (read on the page) says the short bridges 'are all plate girders on masonry abutments' and that some stand on steep grades. No source found says where any of the four stands: Richardson's plan and profile, examined whole, draw no bridge, culvert or stream. One book of 1890, written before the line was finished, counts three bridges, not four (machine text, not checked on the page). This opening falls at about station 455+53 of the 1894 profile, on its 7.80 per cent grade. The three open crossings of Ruxton Creek are inferred to be three of the four bridges; the fourth is not known. This opening is one candidate, and where the line crosses Ruxton Creek in the lower canyon, under fill today, is the other. That this was a bridge of 1890 is conjecture; the opening itself is where the pin says. The line was rebuilt in 2018 to 2021, so what spans each opening today may not be what was built in 1890.
properties.summary: A 33 ft opening under the track over a dry side gully. One of two candidates for the cog road's fourth iron bridge; no source decides.

properties.name: Mount Manitou incline, lower station
properties.basis: Foot of the incline's straight cut where the slope begins above Ruxton Avenue, on a 280 m2 levelled area at 6,609 ft (lidar); the 1948 sheet starts the INCLINE RAILWAY here at BM 6570. The Gazette of 9 July 1908 (read on the page) puts the lower station 150 ft west of the Ute Iron Spring.
properties.summary: The foot of the Mount Manitou incline, beside the cog road's depot on Ruxton Avenue.

properties.name: Mount Manitou incline, upper station
properties.basis: Top of the straight climb where the grade eases from over 50 to about 25 per cent (8,564 ft); OpenStreetMap ends the steps here. No levelled pad is distinct on the lidar; the 1948 sheet marks the top with a building symbol. What stood here has not been read up.
properties.summary: The top of the Mount Manitou incline, on the shoulder of Mount Manitou at about 8,564 ft.

properties.name: Red Mountain incline, lower station
properties.basis: Foot of the straight cut at Ruxton Avenue's level (6,399-6,410 ft); a 185 m2 level patch at 6,399 ft lies 25 ft north-west. The 1948 sheet starts the abandoned line at the street here. A newspaper of January 1912 (machine text, not checked on the page) puts the lower station 'opposite the Catholic church' on Ruxton Avenue.
properties.summary: The foot of the Red Mountain incline at Ruxton Avenue.

properties.name: Red Mountain incline, upper station and pavilion
properties.basis: Where the straight line meets the crest (7,318 ft), 55 ft east of the summit knob (7,331 ft on the lidar; the 1948 sheet's spot height 7360). The knob's small level top (about 120 m2) is the likely site; no distinct pad. A newspaper of July 1925 (machine text) speaks of 'a dance pavilion at the top of the mountain', and a library caption of a small observatory; neither building's footing was picked out on the lidar. Emma Crawford's grave was on this summit; a report of 1929 that its slab was destroyed after the incline was built is hearsay.
properties.summary: The top of the Red Mountain incline, beside the summit knob, where a dance pavilion stood.

properties.name: Red Mountain incline's bridge over the Colorado Midland
properties.basis: The incline's straight line crosses the Colorado Midland's bench and cut (atlas line crossed at 38.857456 N, 104.923280 W); the incline, built about 1912 across a working railway, must have passed over it. The ends are at 38.857538, -104.923307 and 38.857328, -104.923238, good to about 25 ft each. Nothing of a bridge is seen on the lidar. A library's caption (the picture not viewed) speaks of 'a wooden bridge ... part of the railway', which may be this crossing or the hollow higher up. The government sheet of 1948 draws the abandoned line across the Midland here.
properties.summary: Where the Red Mountain incline crossed above the Colorado Midland's cut, about 79 ft, near the foot of the line. Inferred; gone.

properties.name: Ruxton Creek under the cog road in the lower canyon (a candidate for the fourth bridge; under fill today)
properties.basis: The drawn line crosses Ruxton Creek here, about 1,720 ft above the depot (station 443+41 of the 1894 profile, on its 15.80 per cent grade); OpenStreetMap carries the creek under the line as a culvert, and on the 1 m lidar the ground is whole over it, so there is no opening to pin by its ends. Richardson's paper of 1894, p. 419 (read on the page), has 'four iron bridges, two of 20 feet and two of 30 feet span' on granite masonry, and culverts 'all built of red spruce logs'; the Railroad Gazette of 4 April 1890 (read on the page) says the short bridges 'are all plate girders on masonry abutments' and that some stand on steep grades. No source found says where any of the four stands: Richardson's plan and profile, examined whole, draw no bridge, culvert or stream. One book of 1890, written before the line was finished, counts three bridges, not four (machine text, not checked on the page). The three open crossings of Ruxton Creek higher up are inferred to be three of the four bridges. This is the main creek, and the line of 1890 had to cross it here by a bridge or a log culvert; that it was the fourth iron bridge, later buried in fill, is conjecture. The other candidate is the open gap over a dry gully a tenth of a mile above the depot. The line was rebuilt in 2018 to 2021.
properties.summary: Where the line first crosses Ruxton Creek, a third of a mile above the depot. A culvert under fill today; one of two candidates for the fourth iron bridge of 1890.

properties.name: Timber Line (Pikes Peak cog road)
properties.basis: Richardson's profile of 1894 letters 'Timber Line' between stations 139+00 and 144+00 (read on the page), and his text puts timber line 14,700 ft from the top at 11,630 ft (machine text, not checked on the page). The time cards give Timber Line as 2.87 miles of rail from the summit, which is about 14,700 ft on the level: the two agree. The point is 14,700 ft from the summit along the drawn line. Above about 10,500 ft the profile and the drawn line fit less well, to 100 ft or more, hence the wide error. Whether there was a platform or only a name is not known.
properties.summary: A stop on the railway's time cards, 2.87 miles from the summit, where the trees end.

properties.name: Foot of the Pikes Peak carriage road, Cascade
properties.summary: Where the carriages for the summit set out, on Prairie Avenue near the hotel, from 1888.
properties.basis: The north end of today's Prairie Street, where the lane up the hillside begins. The newspapers of 1888 and 1889 (machine text, not checked on the page) start the road on Prairie Avenue near the hotel, a quarter mile from the Midland depot; the sheet of 1909 has the summit road leave the village here. The carriage line met the Midland trains; the fare was $5 from Cascade with the toll, or $2 toll for a private rig. The road was built in 1888 by Carlile, Price and McGavock of Pueblo for the Cascade Town Company and opened with a press excursion on 6 September 1888. The road is drawn 17.2 miles long; the papers of 1888 to 1890 give 16, 17, and 17 miles 400 ft.

properties.name: Toll gate of the carriage road (about here; not located)
properties.summary: The carriage road's toll house, somewhere in Cascade Canyon. Not found; the sources disagree by two miles.
properties.basis: Not located; the pin marks the neighbourhood only. A figure of 1894 puts the toll gate at 8,500 ft, which on the drawn line is about two miles from Cascade, and the Engineering Record of 1915 (read on the page) has a 'Toll Gate Point' near the end of the highway's second mile: the pin is there. Against it, the Rocky Mountain News of 8 September 1888 puts the toll house 3 to 4 miles out, at the top of Cascade Canyon (machine text). The 'Toll Gate' lettered on the map of 1948 at the hairpin above Cascade is the automobile highway's, not this one. William Henry Jackson photographed the gate; a picture may place it.

properties.name: Half Way House of the carriage road (about here; not located)
properties.summary: Gaynor's Half Way House, the relay station where horses were changed for mules, about eight miles from Cascade. Not found.
properties.basis: Not located. The newspapers of 1888 and 1889 (machine text) put the Half Way House about 8 miles from Cascade, two and a half miles after the road leaves the canyon at five. The pin is at today's Halfway picnic ground, 7.5 miles along the drawn line, which fits; but the picnic ground is also half way up the automobile highway and may take its name from that. The record helper inferred Glen Cove instead, which is 10.5 miles along the line and also called '8 miles' in one source. Not to be confused with the Half-Way House of the cog road or the Half Way house of the Cripple Creek stage road.

properties.name: Glen Cove (Pikes Peak carriage road)
properties.summary: A flat under the crags at the foot of the last climb, named on the map of 1894; a stop on the carriage road and later on the highway.
properties.basis: The government sheet of 1894 letters Glen Cove and marks a building beside the road at the foot of the switchbacks; today's Glen Cove is 800 to 1,100 ft east of that mark, the same place within the old sheet's error. The pin is on the road at today's Glen Cove. The Engineering Record of 1915 (read on the page) gives it as the end of the highway's eleventh mile, 11,450 ft, 'the last of the timbered area'.

properties.name: The 'W' switchbacks (Pikes Peak carriage road)
properties.summary: The zigzags above Glen Cove by which the road gains the ridge; photographed from 1888 on.
properties.basis: The sheet of 1894 draws a tight set of zigzags here and today's highway has its tightest hairpins at the same place. The Rocky Mountain News of 8 September 1888 (machine text) has the road zigzag in a 'W' with turns widened to 40 ft, at what it guessed was 11,000 ft; these are at 11,500 to 12,000. Which of today's hairpins are the carriage road's own is not known: the highway was relocated throughout.

properties.name: Summit end of the Pikes Peak carriage road
properties.summary: Where the carriages ended, by the Signal Station on the summit.
properties.basis: The sheet of 1894 ends the road in a small loop on the summit beside the end of the cog railway; the pin is the end of today's road. The first excursion of 6 September 1888 drove to the Signal Station (machine text); in August 1888 the War Department had stopped the work for a time at the boundary of its reservation, within two miles of the top. The best day recorded was 29 July 1890, about 108 people; the cog railway reached the summit on 30 June 1891 and the road was little used after 1893 (machine text).
